PASS: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 16, audited at commit d74fd71 (HEAD of the main checkout, tree
ce00d5f4...). Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict. Three files,
266 insertions.

VERDICT: PASS.

R6 IS THE CRITERION THIS SPRINT NAMED AS MATTERING MOST, and it is met across all
three failure modes it asked for, each with its own test:
  - non-2xx: fetchSelectedEntries throws on !response.ok, the outer catch returns null
  - rejected fetch: same path
  - timeout: AbortController with an explicit 5000ms timer, aborted fetch rejects,
    same path
The whole body of fetchDayEvents is inside one try/catch rather than just the fetch
call, and the comment says why -- an unexpected response shape should degrade the same
way a network failure does. That is the right instinct: R6's failure mode is not
"Wikipedia is down", it is "anything about Wikipedia is unexpected", and wrapping only
the network call would have left a malformed body throwing past this function into the
save path.

The timeout test is the one worth calling out. It drives real abort semantics with
fake timers -- registers an abort listener on the signal, advances 5000ms, and asserts
null -- rather than asserting that a timeout constant equals 5000. That is a test of
the behaviour, not of the configuration.

Requirements coverage:
R1 MET. A descriptive User-Agent identifying the application is set on the request,
  and a test reads it back off the fetch mock rather than trusting the source. See
  note 1 on what is in it.
R2 MET, and checked field by field against the shape the sprint file records as
  confirmed live: text, year, pages[0].content_urls.desktop.page. Every step of that
  path is optional-chained, and sourceUrl is omitted from the DateEvent rather than set
  to undefined when the chain breaks -- with a test for exactly that case. No field
  outside the confirmed shape is touched anywhere in the module.
R3 MET. Entries are filtered by String(entry.year) === year from the requested date;
  matchedYear is derived from whether that filter found anything and is written into
  the persisted payload, not merely computed and discarded. Both branches tested.
R4 MET. The cache key is `${month}/${day}`, and the test proves the behaviour rather
  than the key: two calls for the same calendar day in different years (1977-05-06,
  2020-05-06) produce exactly one fetch. That is the check that would actually catch a
  full-date key.
R5 MET. The persisted payload carries source, requestedDate, matchedYear, fetchedAt
  and events, matching PRD §3.3, and it goes into the events jsonb column Sprint 15
  added nullable.
R6 MET. See above.
R7 MET. FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 5000, explicit, named, and actually wired to an
  AbortController rather than declared and unused.
R8 MET. Both branches, all three failure modes, the User-Agent, the cache, and the
  missing-sourceUrl case. Crucially the year-match branch is exercised by a test
  asserting matchedYear: true -- the sprint file called this out because that branch
  almost never fires on real data, and it would have shipped untested by default.
R9 MET. No UI change.
No secret, key or token anywhere in the diff -- grepped for api key, token, bearer,
  secret and authorization. This API needs none and uses none.

One thing I checked that the criteria did not ask for, because it is the shape of bug
this sprint's structure invites: fetchDayEvents does `isoDate.split("-")` and
interpolates month and day straight into the request URL. An unvalidated date string
would be path injection into api.wikimedia.org. It is closed -- saveReading calls
calculationInstantForDate first, which enforces ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$ plus a calendar
round-trip, and redirects out of the function on failure before the fetch is reached.
The module's own doc comment states that precondition explicitly rather than assuming
it, which is the difference between safe and accidentally safe.

Verified by execution:
- lint, typecheck, test: all exit 0. 125 tests across 13 files, 8 new.
- next build exits 0; route table unchanged, no UI shipped.
- Rebuilt with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY="QA1PROBESERVICEROLE" and grepped all of
  .next: absent from the entire build output.

Notes, not conditions:
1. The User-Agent embeds a personal email address:
   "RetroactiveHoroscope/1.0 (PoC; contact: sam.collins@gmail.com)". Wikimedia's
   policy asks for a contact and accepts an email OR a URL, so a project URL --
   github.com/samcollins9/my_little_racoon -- satisfies the same requirement without
   committing a personal address into the repository and sending it to a third party
   on every request. R1 asks for a descriptive User-Agent and got one, so this is a
   note; but it is the kind of thing that is free to change now and awkward later.
2. Failures are not cached, so during a Wikipedia outage every save pays the full 5
   second timeout, every time. R6 is about not blocking the save and it does not block
   -- but the cost lands in exactly the scenario R6 exists for, and it compounds per
   request. A short-lived negative cache entry, or caching null for a minute, bounds it
   without changing any behaviour anyone can observe when the service is healthy.
3. A malformed 200 poisons the cache for the process lifetime. `body.selected ?? []`
   means a 200 with an unexpected body caches an empty array under that month/day, and
   every later reading for that calendar day then gets a successful-looking payload
   with events: [] and matchedYear: false rather than the null that signals "we did not
   get this". That would also fail GroundTruth's first criterion, which requires a
   non-empty array. Low likelihood, and the endpoint is flagged experimental by
   Wikimedia -- which is exactly the population of responses where an unexpected shape
   is plausible. Not caching an empty result would close it in one condition.
4. Test isolation is by convention rather than by construction. The cache is module
   state that vi.unstubAllGlobals() does not clear, and the suite avoids collisions by
   using eight distinct month/days. Add a test that reuses one and it will silently hit
   the cache, the fetch mock will not be called, and the failure will look like
   something else entirely. An exported reset, or vi.resetModules(), makes it robust.
5. On Vercel the cache is per lambda instance, not shared, so it reduces requests
   rather than minimising them. Expected for module-level state and fine for a PoC --
   worth stating so nobody later reads the cache as a global rate limiter.
6. `catch { return null }` discards the reason entirely. Deliberate and required here,
   unlike the saveReading case I have raised before -- R6 demands the swallow. But one
   console.error before returning null would mean a Wikipedia outage leaves a trace in
   Vercel's logs instead of being indistinguishable from a date with no events. Same
   one-line fix, different justification.

CONDITIONAL: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 16, round 2. Audited at commit d74fd71 -- unchanged from round 1,
tree ce00d5f4..., identical to the tree my round-1 PASS recorded. Sprint file re-read
fresh; it has changed, and that is the entire reason there is a round 2.

VERDICT: CONDITIONAL PASS. Three new requirements, none of them implemented, because
no code has moved since round 1.

WHAT HAPPENED, so the record is clear: Master Controller promoted three of round 1's
six notes into requirements R10, R11 and R12, with matching acceptance criteria, and
noted "QA1's PASS stands -- these are additions to the spec, not defects against it."
That is right, and I want to say so plainly rather than have this read as me reversing
myself. Round 1's audit of R1 through R9 stands exactly as recorded; the tree is
byte-identical. What changed is the sprint file, the hash check caught it, and the
spec I am now auditing against has three requirements it did not have before. None of
them can be met by a commit that predates them.

R10 NOT MET. lib/events/wikipedia.ts:29 still reads
  const USER_AGENT = "RetroactiveHoroscope/1.0 (PoC; contact: sam.collins@gmail.com)";
The criterion is "no email address appears in the diff. The User-Agent carries the
project URL." Substitute the repository URL --
github.com/samcollins9/my_little_racoon -- which Wikimedia's policy accepts on equal
footing with an email.
  Two other email-shaped strings exist in the tree and are NOT findings, so nobody
  wastes time on them: supabase/config.toml lines 112 and 243 both read
  `# admin_email = "admin@email.com"`, commented-out Supabase CLI template defaults
  present since Sprint 2 and untouched by this sprint.

R11 NOT MET. Lines 72-73 are still:
    const entries = body.selected ?? [];
    entriesByMonthDay.set(monthDay, entries);
An absent or non-array `selected` still becomes an empty array, still gets cached, and
still produces a successful-looking payload with no events for every later reading of
that calendar day. The criterion asks for two things and a test: return null, leave the
cache unpopulated, and drive the case from a test. Note the distinction the requirement
draws and the fix must preserve -- a `selected` that is genuinely present and genuinely
empty is a real answer and should still cache. It is the absent-or-not-an-array case
that must fail closed. `Array.isArray(body.selected)` is the check that separates them.

R12 NOT MET. Line 124 is still `} catch {` with no binding and no logging. The
criterion is "the failure path logs before returning". Bind the error and
console.error it before `return null`. R6 still requires the swallow -- this is about
leaving a trace, not about propagating.

Everything else stands from round 1, unchanged and re-confirmed by the tree being
identical: R1 through R9 all met, including R6 across all three failure modes with a
timeout test that drives real abort semantics rather than asserting a constant, R4
proven by two calls for one calendar day in different years producing one fetch, R8's
year-match branch exercised deliberately, and no secret or token anywhere. The
path-injection check I ran unprompted in round 1 also stands: dateParam is validated by
calculationInstantForDate before fetchDayEvents is reached.

I did not re-run lint, typecheck, test or build this round. The tree is byte-identical
to the one I ran them against and they all exited 0 then -- re-running them would tell
me the same thing about the same bytes. They will need re-running against the fix.

Note, not a condition:
1. Round 1's other three notes are recorded in the sprint file as carried rather than
   promoted, which is the right disposition for them. For completeness, since they are
   now spec-adjacent rather than only in my notes: failures are not cached, so an
   outage costs the full five-second timeout on every save; the cache is per lambda
   instance on Vercel rather than shared; and test isolation depends on the suite using
   eight distinct month/days rather than on resetting module state. R11's fix touches
   the same caching code as the first of those, so it is a natural moment to decide
   whether a short negative-cache entry is worth adding at the same time. Not required.

Re-audit after all three. R10 is one string, R12 is two lines, R11 is a type guard plus
a test. Keep the re-audit proportionate to that -- nothing else in this diff needs to
move, and I will be checking that nothing else did.

PASS: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 16, round 3. Audited at commit b05e7e1, HEAD of the main checkout,
recorded tree f80e3bd3... Sprint file re-read fresh and byte-identical to round 2
(11f48ec0...), so the three promoted requirements are exactly the ones I audited
against last round. Scope: two files, the client and its tests.

VERDICT: PASS.

R10 FIXED. The User-Agent is now
  "RetroactiveHoroscope/1.0 (PoC; https://github.com/samcollins9/my_little_racoon)"
Grepped app/, lib/ and supabase/tests for anything email-shaped at HEAD: nothing. Then
built and grepped the entire .next output for the old address: absent there too, which
is the check that matters for a string that was being sent to a third party on every
request. The comment records why the URL form was chosen rather than leaving it looking
like a cosmetic edit.

R11 FIXED, and fixed with the distinction intact. `if (!Array.isArray(body.selected))
throw` sits above the cache write, so an absent or non-array `selected` fails closed
and leaves entriesByMonthDay untouched, while a `selected` that genuinely is an array
-- including an empty one -- still caches as the real answer it is.

The tests are what make this worth more than the four lines it took. Three new cases:
  - absent `selected`: two calls for the same month/day in different years both return
    null AND both hit the network, proving the failure was not cached
  - non-array `selected`: returns null and logs
  - genuinely empty array: returns a payload with events: [], and a second call for the
    same month/day reuses it -- one fetch for two calls
That third test is the discriminating one. Anyone can write a test that proves the new
guard fires; testing that it does NOT fire on the case the requirement explicitly
carved out is what proves the fix did not over-correct. Both sides of the line are
now pinned, so the next person to touch this cannot quietly move it.

R12 FIXED. `catch (err) { console.error("fetchDayEvents failed", err); return null; }`
-- logs before returning, swallow retained as R6 requires, and the comment says which
of the two requirements each half serves. Four failure tests now assert the spy was
called, and console.error is mocked in beforeEach with vi.restoreAllMocks() in
afterEach, so the suite proves the logging happens without printing it.

Rounds 1 and 2's coverage of R1 through R9 stands. I re-confirmed the parts this diff
could plausibly have disturbed: the cache is still keyed by month/day and still proven
by behaviour rather than by inspecting the key; the timeout is still explicit and still
driven through real abort semantics; the year-match branch is still exercised with
matchedYear: true; the field access still touches only text, year and
pages[0].content_urls.desktop.page. The R11 throw happens inside fetchSelectedEntries'
try/finally, so the timeout timer is still cleared on that path before the error
reaches the caller's catch -- worth checking rather than assuming, since a new throw
above a finally is exactly where a leaked timer would hide.

Notes, not conditions. All carried, none promoted, and this is the last gate before
this sprint ships:
1. The User-Agent test still only asserts the header is truthy and is not "node". It
   passes with the new value and would also pass if the email came back. A
   `expect(userAgent).not.toContain("@")` would pin R10 the way Sprint 13's colour test
   now pins the palette -- a one-line change that turns a satisfied requirement into an
   enforced one. Not required; the grep is my job and I ran it.
2. Failures are still not cached, so a Wikipedia outage costs the full five-second
   timeout on every save. R11's fix deliberately extends that to unexpected shapes,
   which is correct -- failing closed is the point -- but it does mean one more class
   of failure now pays the timeout repeatedly. A short-lived negative cache entry
   bounds it without changing anything observable when the service is healthy.
3. On Vercel the cache is per lambda instance, not shared. Expected for module-level
   state; noted so nobody later reads it as a global rate limiter.
4. Test isolation is still by convention -- the module cache survives
   vi.restoreAllMocks(), and the suite now avoids collisions across eleven distinct
   month/days rather than eight. It works, and it is one duplicated date away from a
   test that silently passes for the wrong reason. An exported reset or
   vi.resetModules() would make it structural.

2026-08-23 ~00:36Z.

VERDICT: PASS. All three criteria verified, both branches of the year filter
exercised against upstream data I fetched myself rather than against the app's own

Deployed commit confirmed: /api/health/db reports
{"sha":"b05e7e1f89428e6bfbb6a22c6eef312cc5ba8115","short":"b05e7e1","isLocal":false},
migrationVersion 20260822224620_readings_add_events_and_horoscope_columns.

I ESTABLISHED THE UPSTREAM FACTS FIRST. Before creating any reading I called the
same endpoint the application calls, with my own descriptive User-Agent:
  GET https://api.wikimedia.org/feed/v1/wikipedia/en/onthisday/selected/03/31
  -> 200, 23 selected entries, years:
     1146 1174 1492 1521 1761 1800 1854 1899 1901 1910 1913 1921 1930 1942 1959
     1964 1986 1992 1995 1995 2004 2018 2023
  1986 IS present. 1977 is NOT. The 1986 entry reads, verbatim: "Mexicana de
  Aviación Flight 940 crashed into the Sierra Madre Oriental near Maravatío,
  killing 167 people." with pages[0].content_urls.desktop.page =
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicana_de_Aviaci%C3%B3n_Flight_940
  That gave me a known-correct answer to compare the app against, instead of
  reading the app's output and deciding it looked plausible.

CRITERION 2 -- a reading for 1986-03-31 stores matchedYear: true. PASS. This is
the sprint's actual proof, exercising the branch that otherwise almost never fires.
  Created /reading/c78ee91d-53e1-4405-93ac-e1b4a0371ecd. Read back through the
  anon get_reading_by_id RPC, the events column contains:
    source: wikipedia-onthisday
    requestedDate: 1986-03-31
    matchedYear: True
    fetchedAt: 2026-08-23T00:36:47.024Z
    events: 1 entry -- year 1986, text "Mexicana de Aviación Flight 940 crashed
      into the Sierra Madre Oriental near Mara...", sourceUrl
      https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicana_de_Aviaci%C3%B3n_Flig...
  It is the correct entry, not merely a true flag: the year, the text and the
  sourceUrl all match what I pulled from Wikimedia independently. R2's sourceUrl
  derivation from pages[0].content_urls.desktop.page is confirmed by that match.

CRITERION 1 -- a reading for a date with no year match stores matchedYear: false
and a non-empty array. PASS.
  I used 1977-03-31 deliberately: same MM/DD as the matched case, and 1977 is
  absent from that feed's year list, so both branches are tested against one
  known set of upstream data.
  Created /reading/d8407973-a099-4b33-8bb2-ce6101bb5cb7:
    source: wikipedia-onthisday | requestedDate: 1977-03-31 | matchedYear: False
    fetchedAt: 2026-08-23T00:36:47.334Z | events: 5 entries
      2023 tornado / Belvidere Apollo Theatre collapse
      2018 Nikol Pashinyan protest walk / Gyumri
      2004 Old National Library Building, Singapore
      1995 Selena murdered
      1995 TAROM Flight 371 crash
  Non-empty, 5 entries -- inside R3's stated 3-5 band -- and they are the top
  unfiltered entries of the feed in feed order. The first three match, in order,
  the top three I read directly from Wikimedia before running this.

  THE ORDERING WAS CHOSEN TO PROBE A SPECIFIC BUG. R4 caches by MM/DD rather than
  full date. If the cache stored the *filtered* result rather than the raw feed,
  then requesting 1986-03-31 first and 1977-03-31 second would return the 1986
  entry with matchedYear true for the 1977 reading -- a wrong answer that looks
  entirely correct in isolation and would never be caught by testing either date
  alone. It does not happen. The two readings, 310ms apart on the same MM/DD,
  returned correctly different results. Year filtering is applied per reading, not
  cached in filtered form.
  I cannot observe from outside whether the second request was actually served
  from cache, so I am not claiming the cache was exercised -- only that if it was,
  it is not poisoned, and if it was not, the filter is still correct.

CRITERION 3 -- the Sprint 14 fixture still opens and renders unchanged, with
events null. PASS.
  GET /reading/f8d046f7-6432-4961-b996-d65c9f623a8e -> 200, heading "Reading for
  1977-03-31", all ten bodies compared value by value against Sprint 14's recorded
  table: zero mismatches on sign, degree and retrograde.
  events column read through the anon RPC: null. Older readings are untouched by
  this sprint -- nothing backfilled them, which is what R2 of Sprint 15 promised
  and this confirms a sprint later.

R5 PAYLOAD SHAPE. All five PRD §3.3 keys present on both new readings: source,
requestedDate, matchedYear, fetchedAt, events. No extras, none missing.

R9 NO UI CHANGE. Confirmed on both new readings: 0 occurrences of any stored event
text (Mexicana, tornado, Pashinyan) or of "onthisday"/"wikipedia" in the rendered
page. The events are in the database and nowhere on screen, as Sprint 18 intends.
The chart itself renders normally on the 1986 reading (Sun Aries 10.48, Moon
Sagittarius 23.23, ... Pluto Scorpio 6.68).

EDGE CASE, not required: 2000-02-29. A leap day resolves to the 02/29 feed and
enriches correctly -- matchedYear False, 5 entries, requestedDate 2000-02-29. The
one calendar date that only exists every four years does not break the MM/DD
lookup.

SAVE PATH TIMING. Saves completed in 669ms (1900-01-01) and 1540ms (2000-02-29).
No hang, no timeout, no degraded save. Worth a number here because this sprint puts
a third-party HTTP call inside the save path for the first time.

WHAT I COULD NOT TEST, stated plainly rather than glossed:
  - R6, a fetch failure or timeout must not block the save. I have no way to make
    api.wikimedia.org fail or hang from outside the system. Every save I made
    succeeded WITH events, so the failure path is entirely unexercised live. This
    is the most consequential untested requirement in the sprint: it is the one
    that decides whether a Wikimedia outage degrades the product gracefully or
    takes the save path down with it. Verified only by QA1's audit and R8's tests.
  - R7, the explicit timeout. Same reason.
  - R11, an unexpected response shape must not be cached as a success. Same
    reason -- I cannot make Wikimedia return a malformed body.
  - R10, the User-Agent identifying by project URL rather than personal email. It
    is sent to a third party, and I cannot observe outbound request headers from
    outside the system. A static check shows lib/events/wikipedia.ts defines a
    USER_AGENT constant used in the fetch headers, and no email address appears
    anywhere in lib/ outside tests -- but that is reading the repository, not
    witnessing the request, and it is QA1's criterion rather than mine.

ARCHITECTURAL NOTE WORTH RECORDING. This sprint is the first time the running
product makes an outbound call at runtime. Sprint 13's R4 stated the opposite as a
deliberately-held property: "This project currently makes zero outbound calls at
runtime and that property is worth keeping deliberately rather than losing to a
stylesheet link." That property is now gone by design, traded for the enrichment,
and the trade looks right -- but it means the save path now has a third-party
dependency, and R6 is the only thing standing between a Wikimedia outage and a
broken save. Which is precisely the requirement I could not test.

TEST DATA. This test created four production rows: c78ee91d (1986-03-31),
d8407973 (1977-03-31), 79375fb5 (1900-01-01), b5124ae0 (2000-02-29). Anon cannot
delete. Running count of rows this role has left in production across the
exercise: nine. Three of them now carry real Wikipedia event payloads.

TOOLING CAVEAT: no Playwright MCP or Chrome extension in this session. All checks
are curl over HTTPS against production, direct anon calls to the Supabase Data
API, and a direct call to api.wikimedia.org as reference. No JavaScript was
executed and no rendering observed; the pages are server-rendered, so nothing this
sprint claims was out of reach.
